name: New Jersey Pine Barrens (Pinelands National Reserve)
blurb: Fire-loving pitch pine, acid bogs and a hidden aquifer on sugar sand.

tip.title: Take away fire
tip.text: Fire keeps pine forest from turning to oak. Set Fire to -100% and watch pitch pine, then the seed eaters and the predators that depend on them.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Pitch pine
nodes.desc: The dominant tree of the Pine Barrens, growing on dry acidic sands and in swamps. It can resprout from epicormic shoots after fire, and its seeds feed small mammals and birds.

nodes.name: Blackjack oak
nodes.desc: A scrubby oak of dry sandy soils that grows with pitch pine. Its acorns and leaves feed many animals; without fire, oaks tend to replace pines.

nodes.name: Cranberry
nodes.desc: A low trailing shrub of acidic bogs and wet sands. Its berries are eaten by wildlife and it is grown commercially in the region.

nodes.name: Purple pitcher plant
nodes.desc: A carnivorous plant of nutrient-poor acidic bogs. It drowns insects in rainwater held in its leaves and gets nutrients from the community that breaks them down.

nodes.name: Moths and caterpillars
nodes.desc: Caterpillars chew oak and pine foliage. They are an important protein source for birds, lizards and frogs.

nodes.name: White-tailed deer
nodes.desc: The commonest large mammal of the region. It browses shrubs and young trees, including pine seedlings and sprouts.

nodes.name: Eastern gray squirrel
nodes.desc: Eats acorns and tree seeds, and buries nuts for later. A frequent prey of foxes, coyotes and snakes.

nodes.name: Eastern cottontail
nodes.desc: A rabbit that feeds on herbs and, in winter, twigs and bark. It is prey for many predators from snakes to coyotes.

nodes.name: White-footed mouse
nodes.desc: Eats seeds, nuts and berries. A key small-mammal prey for snakes, foxes and coyotes.

nodes.name: Blue jay
nodes.desc: An omnivore that eats acorns and seeds as well as insects such as caterpillars.

nodes.name: Pine Barrens treefrog
nodes.desc: Breeds in shallow acidic pools, and the New Jersey Pine Barrens hold its largest populations. It is a threatened species in the state.

nodes.name: Eastern fence lizard
nodes.desc: A sun-loving lizard of open sandy pine woods that hunts insects. Black racers hunt it.

nodes.name: Northern pine snake
nodes.desc: A big constrictor that hunts mice and other small mammals, often in their burrows. It favours sandy habitat that burns often, and foxes dig up its nests.

nodes.name: Red fox
nodes.desc: An omnivore that eats small mammals, birds, fruit and berries. It is known to raid pine snake nests and hibernation burrows.

nodes.name: Raccoon
nodes.desc: An adaptable omnivore. GloBI records show it eating squirrels, rabbits and birds such as the blue jay.

nodes.name: Turkey vulture
nodes.desc: A soaring scavenger that feeds on carrion such as dead deer and small mammals.

nodes.name: Coyote
nodes.desc: The top mammalian predator in the region. It eats deer, rabbits, squirrels, mice and smaller carnivores.

nodes.name: Timber rattlesnake
nodes.desc: A threatened ambush predator in New Jersey that eats mice, squirrels and rabbits.

nodes.name: Fire
nodes.desc: Frequent fire shapes the region, from dwarf pine forest to oak forest, and pitch pine is adapted to resprout after it. Most fires are of human origin.

nodes.name: Aquifer water
nodes.desc: The Kirkwood-Cohansey aquifer under the Barrens feeds its bogs, swamps and vernal pools.

nodes.name: Sandy acidic soil
nodes.desc: Sandy, acid, nutrient-poor soil is why the region is called the Barrens.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Energy for all the plants of the open pine forest.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Fungi and bacteria break down dead wood, needles and animals, returning nutrients to the soil.
